On Thursday, Sep. 24, the Perlman Teaching Museum hosted an opening reception for a new exhibit titled “Field Notes.” The exhibit features new work by seven Carleton Studio Art faculty members that commemorates the 100th anniversary of the Cowling Arboretum. The first of its kind in Minnesota, the 800-acre “Arb” was incorporated into the college to “develop a demonstration and testing ground for materials of landscape gardening,” according to Harvey Stork. Stork joined Carleton’s faculty in 1920 as a professor of botany and natural history and was very supportive of the Arb’s creation. Today, it hosts a multitude of recreational, academic and conservation opportunities that encourage students to interact with the local landscape.
The art department does a faculty art showcase about every four years, so, when it came time to develop a new exhibit, many in the department decided the Arb centennial was a worthy theme. Department Chair Kelly Connole’s work often deals with biological and geological subject matter, but she found the intersection of human timekeeping and natural timescales a particularly interesting contrast to explore for this event. Her piece “Bones: An Invitation” combines local materials, such as clay harvested in the Arb, with ready-made objects like bone china dishes and a taxidermied Bison head sourced from her childhood home.
“A hundred years is significant; it does matter, but, in terms of the Arb, it is such a scratch in the surface in terms of geological time,” she said. “There is complexity to time and how we record it.”
The ceramic cups Connole produced for the exhibit were fired in Carleton’s very own wood kiln, which she says is an important tool for connecting students to the local environment and the greater history of ceramic artistry.
“For me at least, I could not teach the history of ceramics and firing theory as well if I did not have that kiln. That deep, deep engagement for a first-year student that comes and spends twenty hours at the kiln — I can’t replace that experience,” said Connole. Her ceramics class also involves students sourcing their own clay directly from the arboretum’s supply.
The kiln runs on wood cutoffs from the art department’s sawmill, which is celebrating its own 20-year anniversary. Students use the sawmill to convert wood collected from maintaining the Arb into tables or sculptural pieces, all while learning about wood-cutting techniques and sustainable forest management. Professor Stephen Mohring, who specializes in sculpture, noticed that students naturally shifted away from more commercial, economical wood designs to ones that showed a more developed understanding of the material once they began working with the sawmill.
“That kind of depth of time in the relationship to the material really actively changed the types of designs that were coming out of the students to things that were far more meaningful and far more personal than they were before the sawmill came onboard,” said Mohring.
It is unique for a college of Carleton’s size to house a wood kiln and a sawmill. “It’s illogical in many ways that we have them, and also really wonderful,” said Connole.
In response to the centennial, Mohring, who often works with natural materials and subject matter, selected works that discuss the passage of time. Viewers of his cross section of a tree from on-campus can track the years back through the pattern of the tree’s rings. That tree, in particular, held a personal connection to Mohring, as it stood next to Boliou Hall for as long as he has worked there. He fashioned the exhibit benches out of slabs from trees up to 130 years old. “Having these things that were longer than the centennial that we were celebrating seemed important,” Mohring said.
To highlight more current developments in the local environment, Mohring started a livestream from the old location of the Carleton weather station in the Arb. “[Using outside data] felt almost like cheating to me. I had this place where there was all this data, that was actually in the arboretum, that I could use,” said Mohring.
This isn’t the first faculty showcase themed around the local wilderness, and many works in the exhibit highlight the history of collaboration between art faculty and the arboretum management.
Hsar Sar Lwin, an educational assistant for the Carleton art department, said, “It was really cool to see pieces that used material from the arb and learn about this ongoing relationship the art department has with the Arb. It makes me more aware of how precious material is and how we should minimize waste.”
Those interested in hearing more about the creative processes of the participating faculty can attend the upcoming artist talks, beginning with Eleanor Jensen and Stephen Mohring on Oct. 9 at 4:00 p.m. in the Perlman Teaching Museum.

Every August, campus rumbles with the beginnings of a new school year: dorms get cleaned, NSW leaders get trained and, of course, packages pile up in the Great Hall. Most Carleton students don’t think much about picking up a package at Carleton or checking their mailbox, but getting everything where it needs to go is a lot more complicated than most students assume. So, what are the actual processes behind Carleton’s mail system?
In general, mail usually gets to Carleton in one of three ways: United States Postal Service (USPS), FedEx or UPS. Every morning (except on Sundays), a delivery truck for each service pulls up to the loading dock under Sayles-Hill. Student workers help unload several carts of staff and student mail and hand over any outgoing mail. Then, student workers move these carts full of letters and boxes up to the mailroom using the elevator. Once upstairs, workers sort through the mail, separating student mail from staff mail and “routing” them through the mailroom tracking app QTrack.
Sal LaMotte ’30 brought up a common student complaint about deliveries taking a long time. However, once a package actually reaches Carleton’s loading dock, it is routed within the same day, often within thirty minutes of delivery.
The routing process is what tells the QTrack system to email a specific student that they’ve received a package and it also allows mail workers to locate specific packages when a student comes to pick it up. A student worker writes the recipient’s last name and first initial, along with the date received, on the side of the package before scanning it into the system. The program then emails the student listed as the recipient, including a place to scan a barcode indicating where the package has been placed. Possible locations include the shelves, small or medium bins, or, for the largest packages, either the back hall (the area behind the mailboxes) or the loading dock downstairs.
“I had my bike shipped here from home,” said LaMotte, which is one example of a package large enough to remain at the loading dock.
With a peak of over 1000 packages at the start of this year, the whole operation moves to the Great Hall in August and only returns to the regular mailroom — which only has capacity for about 400 packages — in late September.  LaMotte said that he had had “packages delivered before school started, which was very helpful.”
This is a fairly typical practice for students to do and contributes to that August and early September boom. While routing and delivering packages takes a lot of time, student workers also have other jobs. Hazel Wright ’28 has been a student worker in the mailroom for just over two years, including working one spring break and two summer breaks.
Wright said her duties “depend on what time of day my shift is and [they are] different over breaks.” She said they could include “sorting letter mail, labeling packages, [being a] campus driver, trips and lifting heavy things as needed,” she said.
Letter mail is what students typically receive inside their mailboxes. It needs to be sorted alphabetically every day before being placed in mailboxes from behind. This also involves sorting through all the mail for people that do not have a listed mailbox. This could happen for a variety of reasons: mail delivered to a graduated senior, someone off-campus for a study abroad program or simply someone unrelated to Carleton whose letter was misdelivered. Because student letter mail doesn’t come with an email notification, it can often sit for a while.
“I do check my mailbox, [but] not very often because I’m not expecting mail very much,” LaMotte said.
Many students are not as judicious as LaMotte, evidenced by the Friday flowers delivered the first week that are wilting inside mailboxes well into Week 4.
While students get mail delivered to their mailboxes in Sayles, student workers hand-deliver faculty and staff mail on one of five trips. The first four trips are walking routes that go to various areas around campus, though some are better done by bike. Those routes generally stop in each department’s lounge or receiving area where their incoming and outgoing mail trays are kept. The fifth trip, dubbed the Ole Run, is done in the mail vehicle. The Ole Run goes to farther-flung buildings like the Rec Center and the stadium as well as all the way up to St. Olaf itself. Carleton and St. Olaf often receive mail for each other, so this daily exchange solves that problem. Because of these trips, student mail workers can become very familiar with professors and their departments without ever meeting them in person.
But student workers are not the only ones who keep the mailroom running. David Entenmann is the Mail Services Coordinator and directs all student workers. He has been at Carleton for nine years, since spring of 2019. He has chosen to stay here because he has “a strong connection to higher education” and he enjoys “interacting with the students.” He added that working here is “a job with a lot of varied tasks,” where he can “use various skills he’s developed.” Wright also said this variety is a major reason she has stayed for several years.
Wright did, however, bring up the lack of scaled pay as a challenge for student workers in the mailroom. Wright has worked in the mailroom for several years and has also worked over breaks. She currently serves in essentially a “mini manager[ial]” role, including training new workers and being the point of reference for any questions during everyday operations. She explained that if student workers received “higher pay for being here longer [they] could retain more people” and would not “have to train up an entire new crop of first years” while simultaneously dealing with “not enough experienced workers overlapping.”
Entenmann also commented on common issues with student mail, reminding students to “please have your full and complete name” on all mail and to address everything to the 300 N College Street address (and not the 1N address as that is reserved for faculty). He also reminds students not to “ship things to your dorms,” but that non-mail items like grocery deliveries should be going to dorms rather than the mailroom.
Entenmann also revealed that while letter mail has decreased by 70% since COVID-19 as departments switched to email during the pandemic, “incoming packages have gone way up and are being delivered in a lot more varied ways” than they used to be. So, while snail mail may be less popular in the era of email, the mailroom still has a great deal to do.

Oct. 1, 2026, marked the first Night Owls of the fall term: a “new student-focused discussion series happening twice this term.” This was an opportunity for students who still enjoy reading or have some interest in it. There was also Domino’s pizza for students to grab and eat while holding conversation. This meeting, hosted by Philosophy Professor Daniel Groll and President Alison Byerly, was an opportunity for students to converse about reading habits.
Byerly was very open about her views on literature and how she admires people who even make the effort to try and read more. Allex Tran ’28, a volunteer, said that he “came [to the event] to see the President’s perspective on literature” and hear the opinions of his other peers.
The dynamic continued with the hosts posing questions for students to discuss in groups or partners before sharing their thoughts with the rest of their peers. One such discussion focused on the role that reading still has in our lives.
“Even though it was very late and I could’ve used that time to do other work or even prepare myself for the upcoming day, I enjoyed how there was something school-related that had nothing to do with school,” said Andy Nguyen ’30.
The Night Owls went from conversations to questions, even analyzing an excerpt from Middlemarch by George Elliot. President Byerly discussed the notion that some people dislike analyzing literature because it requires deep and strenuous thinking, which may make reading literature difficult to enjoy. However, as she invited students to speak up, most of them disagreed; they stated how good literature can be analyzed and thus be entertaining.
Nia Rose ’30 emphasized how she would “totally attend the upcoming Night Owls events.” She also mentioned finding the event engaging because its discussion included students from all years and faculty members, and it occurred in a casual setting outside of the classroom.
In the end, Tran said that, after this discussion, he was able to “find new ideas and even revisit old ones” about his views on literature. Groll hopes to bring even more students together for the next iteration of Night Owls, which will occur around Week 5 or 6.
